paper_summary: This paper introduces GRADINO, a from-scratch benchmark generator and evaluation framework for numerical question answering over multiple non-relational tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (used for executable SQL supervision and gold answers), then renders answer-preserving perturbed non-relational views (pivots/hierarchical headers, merged cells, blank rows/cols, typographical noise, unit conversions, footnotes) and verbalizes SQL programs into natural-language questions. It supports two multi-table evidence-flow topologies: parallel (independent scalar extraction then aggregation) and sequential (lookup-chains where intermediate results parameterize later queries). The authors evaluate LLMs (gpt-5-mini and Qwen variants) across environmental and financial domains, varying table count (2–20), aggregation operators, and unit heterogeneity. Key findings: accuracy degrades sharply with table count and unit heterogeneity (especially in the environmental domain with physical unit conversions), sequential chains are harder than parallel aggregation, and non-relational presentation amplifies errors in multi-table scenarios. They also show generated data can augment scarce in-domain supervision and provide manual verification of question fidelity (≈95.9% correct on a sample). The paper includes thorough appendices documenting prompts, constraints, solver-backed sampling, and real-table validation.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Addresses an important and under-explored blind spot: multi-table numerical reasoning over non-relational (presentation-encoded) tables. 2) Elegant methodological design: decoupling an executable latent relational source (SQL supervision) from perturbed non-relational renderings preserves verifiability while allowing controlled perturbations. 3) Comprehensive generation pipeline: schema generation, solver-backed semantic constraints for plausibility, answer-preserving rendering (pivots/hierarchical headers, unit conversions, noise), and NL verbalization with verification. 4) Strong empirical results: systematic experiments across models, domains, table counts and unit settings that reveal large, consequential failure modes (scaling collapse and unit-heterogeneity collapse). 5) Practical utility: GRADINO data can augment scarce in-domain training and improves downstream performance. 6) Reproducibility-friendly documentation: extensive prompts and appendix material; stated release of code and datasets.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Limited synthetic realism: GRADINO is a controlled synthetic generator and cannot capture all visual, distributional, or domain idiosyncrasies of real-world documents (e.g., alignment cues, charts, OCR artifacts). The paper acknowledges this, but broader real-world validation would strengthen external validity. 2) Verbalization dependence: NL questions are LLM-generated and verified by an LLM; despite a good manual pass rate, question verbalization remains a source of potential errors (particularly for sequential questions where constraints may be dropped). 3) Domain and model coverage: experiments focus on two domains and a modest set of LLMs, limiting claims about universality across other domains (scientific, industrial) or other model families. 4) Generator-model coupling risk: GRADINO uses an LLM to generate the latent source and uses gpt-5-mini in evaluation; although authors discuss and partially mitigate overlap, further cross-generator experiments would reassure against distributional bias favoring generator families. 5) Perturbation scope: visual/layout phenomena (fonts, alignment cues) and multimodal/OCR renderings are not fully modeled; these are relevant in many real deployments. 6) Diagnostic granularity: the metric (2-decimal EM) is appropriate for numerical QA, but more detailed error decomposition (retrieval vs normalization vs arithmetic) would improve interpretability of failure modes.
comments_suggestions_typos: Minor suggestions: 1) Increase human verification sample (especially for sequential cases) to better quantify NL fidelity across settings. 2) Consider generator ablations using different LLMs to measure sensitivity to generator choice. 3) Provide more error-type analysis separating retrieval, normalization, and arithmetic failures so users know where to focus engineering effort. 4) If feasible, extend rendering to image/OCR variants to connect with vision+LLM table understanding. 5) Ensure final release includes runnable scripts, seeds, and quickstart instructions. Typos/edits: generally well written; suggest consistent capitalization of model names in captions and a quick pass for minor layout hyphenation issues.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors discuss limitations and societal impacts responsibly in §6 and the ethics section: GRADINO generates synthetic non-identifying data, only uses public real tables for validation, and they note synthetic realism limitations. The paper could expand on domain biases introduced by synthetic lexica and on how benchmarks should not be mistaken for guarantees of real-world reliability; they mention this but further guidance/examples could help practitioners. Overall, the discussion is adequate.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical concerns. The benchmark uses synthetic fictional entities for generation and public datasets only for validation; privacy issues are appropriately addressed. The authors acknowledge risks about interpretive misuse (over-confidence in synthetic benchmark performance).
